To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
multinationals' HRM practices can be understood as an important player within a network of economic and social actors.

multinationals and local skills policy actors are embedded in a network of social relations, that the social structure within this network shapes the way in which multinationals engage with local skills actors and that this engagement is a process through which the multinationals partially endogenize the local labour market skills resources.

the subsidiaries of foreign MNCs engage with labour market skill actors, and that the power structures mobilised by local actors to align labour markets with the demands of MNCs may result in resource endogenization.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how HRM can contribute to the development of a more socially embedded perspective on the labour market.
the ways in which HRM may become implicated in the social and economic sustainability of the local economy.
the ways that MNCs and other actors mobilize power in the labour market and how this is shaped by the social structure of institutional governance arrangements.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this paper provides a theoretical framework to understand how HRM agency can be mobilised in the external labour market.

MNCs' engagement with the external labour market is shaped by a complex interaction between the social structures of the local institutional governance arrangements and the strategic action of the MNCs.

this paper has shown the importance of the embeddedness framework in the analysis of the role of HRM in the labour market, and that it is a valuable tool for understanding the role of HR in the wider social context.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we show how the social structure of local skills governance arrangements can create a space for multinationals to engage in social concerns through the strategic management of their skills requirements.
the social structure is an essential mechanism for the mobilisation of social resources, and that the mobilisation of such resources is essential for endogenizing the external labour market.
we have shown that MNCs are not only embedded in the local labour markets in which they operate, but that they can also be active agents of change within them.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the social structure and strategic action of firms and local labour market skills actors can be mobilised to create a conduit for resource endogenization, and that this is likely to occur when actors are able to align their economic and social interests.

MNCs' agency in the external labour market is not simply a product of their own strategic action but of the social structure of local institutional governance arrangements and the strategic actions of local actors.
MNCs may be a key actor in the social construction of the external labour market.
